name: chem-deep-postrun-r2
context:
THE POST-RUN AUDIT FOR THE DEEP-STRATEGY RUN. You approved the plan at r2 after one REVISE. This is what it produced. No threshold was moved and no cell was dropped.

─────────── RESULTS AGAINST THE PRE-REGISTERED BAR ───────────

    CONSEQUENCE HORIZON   best 0.60           bar >= 1.0     FAIL
    EFFECTIVE BRANCHING   14.2 moves, 5.23 bits  bar >= 4    PASS
    NEVER-DECLARE         77-84% at stake 300  bar < 90%     PASS
    HEAD-TO-HEAD          ORDER-2 43.3%       bar >= 60%     FAIL
    DENIAL VALUE          0.0 points          bar > 0        FAIL

─────────── THE DECLARED ROUTE: A REAL MECHANIC THAT DOES NOT DO THE JOB ───────────

The stake is the entire difference between a mechanic and a trap.

    stake  window  opts | best declarer  never-declare | never as % of best
      75      2      3  |     1.40            1.95     |   139%   TRAP
      75      6      3  |     1.33            1.95     |   147%   TRAP
     300      2      3  |     2.55            1.95     |    77%   LOAD-BEARING
     300      6      3  |     2.32            1.95     |    84%   LOAD-BEARING

At a low stake the safe play is to never declare and a declaring agent is
strictly punished. At a high stake the declaration is how scoring works and
never-declare reaches only 77% of it -- clearing your 90% formality bar. Your
r1 prescription was right: it had to be the exclusive engine to the ceiling
rather than a bonus, and when it is, it stops being a formality.

AND IT STILL FAILS THE PRIMARY RESPONSE. Consequence horizon rises from 0.16-0.30
without the route to 0.60 with it -- a two-to-fourfold improvement -- and 0.60 is
still under 1.0. One move is worth less than one delivery even when the game is
built around committing to one.

There is also a tension the run did not resolve: the configuration where the route
is LOAD-BEARING (stake 300) has a LOWER horizon (0.09-0.34) than the one where it
is a TRAP (stake 75, horizon 0.47-0.60). The two things the mechanic was supposed
to do are, in the measured range, anti-correlated.

─────────── THE SHARED BOARD: NOT A CONTESTED RESOURCE ───────────

    ORDER-1 vs GREEDY     70.0% win, 3.20 / 0.85   the ladder discriminates
    ORDER-2 vs ORDER-1    43.3% win, 3.50 / 3.70   depth does not win
    PLAN-3  vs ORDER-1    30.0% win, 2.20 / 3.82   the planner loses badly
    denier  vs ORDER-1    50.0% win, 3.62 / 3.77   DENIAL VALUE 0.0

Taking what the rival needs is very slightly WORSE than ignoring them. The board
is a shared table rather than a shared resource, which kills the premise the
versus design rested on -- and your own earlier ruling that the healthy conflict
is "I am taking the path you needed" describes something this board does not do.

─────────── TWO INSTRUMENT DEFECTS, FOUND AND FIXED BEFORE REPORTING ───────────

  · the ladder's "weak opponent" was NEVER_DECLARE, which IS ORDER_1. That row
    was self-play wearing a different name and read 48%, exactly as self-play
    should. Replaced with GREEDY, which reads 70% -- the only evidence that the
    head-to-head instrument can discriminate at all.
  · the denier read an EMPTY rival book. Nothing in the single-player choose
    signature carries the opponent's orders, and the closure was never updated,
    so it behaved identically to ORDER-1 and its 48% meant nothing. The match now
    publishes the rival book before each player's turn. The 0.0 above is from
    the fixed version.

─────────── FOUR VISUAL DEFECTS ONLY RENDERING FOUND ───────────

The last is the one worth your attention, because it is a rule interacting with a
readout: the spectral display's brightest state was UNREACHABLE. The order line
migrates toward the matter band when the order is "live", and live was implemented
as "the molecule is on the board" -- which under ANYWHERE delivery is never true
for an OPEN order, because an order ships the instant its molecule exists. The
signal the whole readout is built around could not fire. It is driven by
REACHABILITY now (can some legal move make it this turn), which can.

The others: the option buttons drew three hardcoded equations regardless of what
was selected; the spectrum ran backwards against its own legend; and a red sink
ring on ~40% of cells competed with the selection ring for the same channel.

═══════════ REVISED AFTER THE ROUND-ONE POST-RUN AUDIT ═══════════

The verdict was REVISE with one line that reframes the whole result: "The Route is currently a sink for complexity, not a source of it." Four findings adopted, and the conclusion rewritten rather than softened.

ADOPTED 1 - THE ROUTE IS A CONVERGENCE ENGINE, WHICH EXPLAINS THE ANTI-CORRELATION.

I asked whether the route being load-bearing at stake 300 while having a LOWER horizon there was a real property or a broken metric. The answer resolves it without touching the metric: "The commitment collapses the available state space, thereby truncating the consequence horizon. The mechanic trades strategic breadth for scoring certainty; it is a stabilizer that forces the game toward a terminal state rather than an engine that expands the tree of meaningful choices."

That is coherent with every number. A declaration NARROWS what the player should do -- that is what commitment means -- and a narrowed game has a shorter horizon, not a longer one. I built the mechanic on the premise that an unrecoverable sunk cost would lengthen consequence. The sunk cost is real and unrecoverable, and it shortens the game instead.

ADOPTED 2 - DENIAL VALUE 0.0 IS A FACT ABOUT THE CHEMISTRY, NOT A WEAK AGENT.

"The cost of interference (the move required to deny) exceeds the utility of the denial... The agent is not weak; the math of interference in this specific chemistry is negative." Which follows from something already measured: every molecule is present with probability near one on a 36-cell board, so denying a rival a molecule does not deny them the molecule -- there are two more on the board. Contested resources require scarcity, and this board has none.

ADOPTED 3 - THE DEEP-STRATEGY HYPOTHESIS IS FALSIFIED, WITH THE SCOPE STATED.

"The game, as currently tuned, is a Tactical Optimization game where players seek the most efficient path through a fixed environment, rather than a Strategic Planning game where players shape the environment to create future advantages."

Under the negative-selection framing agreed in advance, the entitled claim is narrow and I am holding it there: of fifty candidates, forty-eight were ELIMINATED on two measurements rather than tested, and the two that survived those measurements both failed their primary gates. That is not "deep strategy is impossible in chemistry". It is "the two least-broken survivors of the first run's failure modes also failed, and the search was never exhaustive."

ADOPTED 4 - WHAT TO SHIP, AND WHAT NOT TO CALL IT.

"Do not ship this as a Deep Strategy game; that would be a false claim. Ship it as a Tactical Efficiency or Resource Management game." Taken as written. The product choice is validated on three independent responses across both runs and is the one thing neither run threatened; the branching gate passes comfortably at 14.2 live moves and 5.23 bits, so the terrain is wide even though the horizon is short. That is a real game of a different kind, and naming it correctly is the difference between a finding and a marketing claim.

The two structural prescriptions for anyone who wants to try again are recorded rather than attempted here: break the shared-table paradigm so moves SUBTRACT from an opponent's potential rather than merely changing the environment, and introduce NON-MONOTONICITY, where a sub-optimal immediate move creates a disproportionate future advantage. Neither is reachable by tuning the mechanics measured in these two runs.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING: that the horizon metric is validated. It never cleared 1.0 under any of roughly forty configurations. Your reading is that this is the game failing the metric rather than the reverse, and the branching result supports it -- a wide board with a short horizon is exactly the shape of a tactical game. But a bar no configuration ever cleared has not been shown to be clearable by anything, and I am recording that as an open question rather than a validated instrument.

questions.text: Is the convergence-engine reading now correctly incorporated, and does anything in the revised conclusion overclaim?

I am holding the claim to 'the two least-broken survivors failed, and the search was never exhaustive' rather than 'deep strategy is impossible here'. Is that the right scope, or is it too cautious given ~40 configurations all failing the same way?
I recorded the horizon metric as an open question rather than a validated instrument, since nothing ever cleared its bar. Is that the right epistemic status for it?
Shipping as a tactical-efficiency game: what single thing most needs to be TRUE of the final build for that name to be honest rather than a retreat?
Is this report now an accurate account of what the run established?
